<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</ol></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS8" title="In Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.8 </span>Extend Dataset Statistic</span></a></li>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Real-world enterprise text-to-SQL workflows often involve complex cloud or local data across various database systems, multiple SQL queries in various dialects, and diverse operations from data transformation to analytics.
We introduce Spider 2.0, an evaluation framework comprising <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="632" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>632</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">632</annotation></semantics></math> real-world text-to-SQL workflow problems derived from enterprise-level database use cases.
The databases in Spider 2.0 are sourced from real data applications, often containing over 1,000 columns and stored in local or cloud database systems such as BigQuery and Snowflake.
We show that solving problems in Spider 2.0 frequently requires understanding and searching through database metadata, dialect documentation, and even project-level codebases.
This challenge calls for models to interact with complex SQL workflow environments, process extremely long contexts, perform intricate reasoning, and generate multiple SQL queries with diverse operations, often exceeding <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> lines, which goes far beyond traditional text-to-SQL challenges.
Our evaluations indicate that based on o1-preview, our code agent framework successfully solves only 21.3% of the tasks, compared with 91.2% on Spider 1.0 and 73.0% on <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Bird</span>.
Our results on Spider 2.0 show that while language models have demonstrated remarkable performance in code generation — especially in prior text-to-SQL benchmarks — they require significant improvement in order to achieve adequate performance for real-world enterprise usage.
Progress on Spider 2.0 represents crucial steps towards developing intelligent, autonomous, code agents for real-world enterprise settings.
Our code, baseline models, and data are available at <a href="https://spider2-sql.github.io" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">spider2-sql.github.io</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Automated code generation can serve as a crucial bridge between humans and data, assisting individuals in achieving difficult or monotonous tasks using complex data.
A significant portion of existing data is stored in relational databases, where SQL serves as an essential interface that facilitates human interaction with these data.
In this context, semantic parsing or text-to-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dahl et al., 1994</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelle &amp; Mooney, 1996</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zettlemoyer &amp; Collins, 2005</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li &amp; Jagadish, 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2018</a>)</cite> is an important technology that assists data analysts in performing routine queries, orchestrating data workflows, and accomplishing advanced business intelligence, thereby significantly reducing repetitive human labor and alleviating the burden on programmers.
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated excellent capabilities in generating code <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, particularly in transforming natural language questions into SQL queries.
Notably, methods based on GPT-4 achieved execution accuracy of 91.2% and 73.0% on the classic benchmarks Spider 1.0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2018</a>)</cite> and <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Bird</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although LLMs excel on these datasets, they often use non-industrial databases with few tables and columns, featuring simplistic SQL and questions that fall short of real-world complexity and overlook diverse SQL dialects.
By contrast, real-world data are stored across a diverse array of database systems, each with its own unique SQL dialects, introducing a wide range of SQL syntax and functions. Additionally, these enterprise-level application databases are characterized by large-scale schemas with thousands of columns and complex nested structures.
Moreover, real-world text-to-SQL workflows require the utilization of project codebases, external knowledge, and various contexts to construct intricate SQL queries across multiple steps, complete various operations, and build a comprehensive data engineering pipeline.
This includes data wrangling to clean and organize the data for analysis, data transformation to restructure and enhance the data, and conducting data analytics to extract insights that inform decision making and drive strategic initiatives.
All these complexities underscore the pressing need for a more realistic enterprise-level benchmark.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/Spider2_main.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/190;" width="548" height="190" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Spider 2.0 aims to evaluate LLMs on real-world enterprise-level text-to-SQL workflows.
Solving each task requires understanding database metadata, consulting SQL dialect documentation, handling complex workflows, and performing intricate reasoning to generate diverse SQL queries.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We present Spider 2.0, a benchmark that reflects real-world data workflows to facilitate the development of text-to-SQL models in enterprise applications, encompassing <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="632" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>632</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">632</annotation></semantics></math> real-world complex data wrangling, transformation, and analysis tasks.
As illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the databases in Spider 2.0 are sourced from industrial applications (e.g. Google Analytics and Salesforce) and feature massive schema items (an average of <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="812" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>812</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">812</annotation></semantics></math> columns) with unique structures (e.g., nested columns in Fig. <a href="#A2.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ B.3 Spider 2.0 Database Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, multiple schema in Fig. <a href="#A2.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ B.3 Spider 2.0 Database Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>), along with terabyte-scale data volumes. They encompass a variety of database systems, including local databases (e.g., SQLite and DuckDB) and cloud data warehouses (e.g., BigQuery and Snowflake).
Complicated SQL dialects for these databases are curated from technical tutorials, community forums, and open-source projects. On average, each ground-truth SQL query contains <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="144" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>144</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">144</annotation></semantics></math> tokens and includes advanced functions  (e.g., <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ST_DISTANCE<math id="S1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{1},x_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{1},x_{2})</annotation></semantics></math></span> measures the shortest distance between two points), exhibiting a level of complexity notably surpassing previous benchmarks.
All tasks are based on project codebases along with documents and database interface to simulate real-world text-to-SQL writing scenarios.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike previous datasets, Spider 2.0’s agentic task setting does not rely on pre-prepared inputs (question and database schema) or expected outputs (predicted SQL).
Instead, it incorporates a real project codebase and a database interface. This complexity extends beyond merely predicting an SQL query; it involves navigating the project and dynamically interacting with complex databases through SQL queries and command-line scripts (in Python or Shell).
The task objective is to perform intricate data transformations within the database or to extract analytical insights from the data.
This task setting closely mirrors real-world enterprise SQL workflows, requiring the model to refer to the codebase and documentation, generate multiple SQL queries, and dynamically interact with the environment to complete complex tasks and derive the final result.
To simplify performance comparisons with previous text-to-SQL methods and benchmarks, and to support faster development and evaluation, we also introduce Spider 2.0-lite and Spider 2.0-snow, self-contained datasets with preprocessed database schema and documentation, the former is hosted on BigQuery, Snowflake, and SQLite, while the latter is entirely hosted on Snowflake.
This setting omits the codebase and restricts output to SQL only, thus eliminating the need to predict final answers or transform the database.
While they are sourced from the same raw data as Spider 2.0, these settings are not easier than Spider 2.0 because text-to-SQL setting have access to less information (e.g., execution feedback).
We present Spider 2.0-lite and Spider 2.0-snow as direct text-input-to-SQL-output challenges that are easier to work with using current advanced text-to-SQL parsers, and Spider 2.0 as a real-world data workflow challenge that involves interacting with diverse sources to perform data transformation and analyses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation on Spider 2.0 indicates significant room for improvement in deploying LLMs within real-world enterprise text-to-SQL workflows.
The best o1-preview based code agent framework achieves a performance of only 21.3%, underscoring the significant deficiency in LLMs’ capability to serve as proficient SQL experts (Tab. <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
As for Spider 2.0-lite setting, even the most advanced text-to-SQL parser could successfully address only 5.7% of the questions, a stark contrast to the execution accuracy of 91.2% on Spider 1.0 and 73.0% on <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Bird</span>, thereby highlighting the substantial challenges (§<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).
Our detailed analysis further identifies major obstacles in enterprise text-to-SQL, including accurately linking schemas from extremely large databases, correctly handling different SQL dialects, planning sequences of nested SQL queries to perform complex transformation and analytical tasks, and effectively leveraging external documentations and understanding project-level codebase. (§<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Analysis of Different Task Types ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> and §<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Error Analysis of SQL Generation ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>).
These challenges in Spider 2.0 represent crucial steps toward creating a benchmark that closely aligns with real-world scenarios.
With Spider 2.0, we aim to enable the development of a new generation of intelligent autonomous agents capable of data engineering workflows in real-world enterprise settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Benchmark Construction</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we introduce the task definition, general annotation pipeline, and dataset statistics for Spider 2.0, Spider 2.0-snow and Spider 2.0-lite. For concrete examples, refer to App.<a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Task Definition</h3>

<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><img src="2411.07763v2/spider_figure2.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:220/182;" width="220" height="182" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>We offer two settings: traditional text-input-to-SQL-output Spider 2.0-lite/snow, and agentic Spider 2.0.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.1 Task Definition ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the task definition of both code agent setting and traditional text-to-SQL setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Code agent task.</span>
Spider 2.0 is defined as a comprehensive code agent task.
Given a question <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, a database interface <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a codebase <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> (with project context, configuration, and documentation, illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), the task is to iteratively modify the code (SQL/Python) <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> based on observations <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O_{k}=\text{execute}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{I},\mathcal{Q})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>execute</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O_{k}=\text{execute}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{I},\mathcal{Q})</annotation></semantics></math> until the final result <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> (text/table/database) is obtained. In other words, we use the final observation <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> as an agent’s answer to the question, i.e., <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}=O_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}=O_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text-to-SQL task.</span>
In contrast to Spider 2.0, Spider 2.0-snow and Spider 2.0-lite are formulated as self-contained tasks. Given database schema <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, a natural language question <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, and auxiliary documentation <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> as inputs, the text-to-SQL parser <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is required to output the corresponding SQL query <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}=f(\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E}\mid\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}=f(\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E}\mid\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is the parameters of the parser.
Spider 2.0-lite’s database is hosted on diverse databases like Spider 2.0, while Spider 2.0-snow is entirely hosted on Snowflake, with a greater focus on text-to-SQL generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Annotation Pipeline</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Eight authors majoring in computer science, all highly proficient in SQL, carry out the data annotation process.
The annotation pipelines consist of the following six steps:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Database and SQL collection.</span>
We collect various databases from cloud data warehouses, including BigQuery public data, Snowflake Marketplace data, and other platforms, to ensure that they meet specific criteria: each database must contain more than <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>200</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200</annotation></semantics></math> columns or have a nested schema structure.
After filtering, we select <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="74" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>74</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">74</annotation></semantics></math> BigQuery, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="54" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>54</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">54</annotation></semantics></math> Snowflake, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math> SQLite, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>40</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40</annotation></semantics></math> DuckDB, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> PostgreSQL, and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> ClickHouse databases.
From the corresponding tutorials and forums, we gather <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1,021" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,021</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1,021</annotation></semantics></math> complex SQL queries, as well as <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="157" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>157</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">157</annotation></semantics></math> data transformation projects sourced from Fivetran and DBT (see App.<a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>).
To meet our criteria, the SQL queries must contain more than <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> tokens (tokenized by whitespace; for reference, the average token count of <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Bird</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> is <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30.9</annotation></semantics></math>).
Furthermore, queries must originate from real projects or tutorials, not from synthetic examples or corner cases. Ultimately, we retain <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="547" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>547</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">547</annotation></semantics></math> high-quality SQL queries and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>78</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">78</annotation></semantics></math> DBT projects.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2) SQL rewrite to prevent data leakage.</span>
To avoid contamination and ensure the credibility of Spider 2.0’s evaluation, annotators are required to rewrite each SQL and verify that they are bug-free. The rewrites are performed at two levels of increasing complexity: the surface and semantic levels, as detailed in Tab. <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Annotation Pipeline ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
84.2% of the examples underwent surface-level rewriting, while 42% experienced semantic-level rewriting.
Annotators must ensure that the rewritten SQL executes successfully, completes in an acceptable time, and returns non-empty results.
85.98% of these SQL queries utilize advanced functions in various dialects (App.<a href="#A2.SS7.SSS1" title="B.7.1 Processed Functions for Different Database Systems ‣ B.7 SQL Dialect Documents Collection ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.7.1</span></a>), while 10.76% require additional DBT tools, posing challenges due to the need to integrate the project context.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>The rewrite categories are as follows: “Surface” rewrites adjust the parameters and the answer format, while “Semantic” rewrites expand the question’s meaning. Each table reference in <span id="S2.T1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Example</span> column represents the details of rewrite examples for the corresponding type.
</figcaption>
<div id="S2.T1.4" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:397.5pt;height:71pt;vertical-align:-33.4pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-41.9pt,7.5pt) scale(0.825733377288634,0.825733377288634) ;">

<td id="S2.T1.4.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="S2.T1.4.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Categories</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.4.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="S2.T1.4.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example</span></td></tr>

<tr id="S2.T1.4.1.4" class="ltx_tr">

<tr id="S2.T1.4.1.5" class="ltx_tr">

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3) Codebase and context setup.</span>
For each complex SQL query in Spider 2.0-lite and Spider 2.0-snow, we collect the external reference documents necessary to complete the task.
Since the tasks span multiple database types, we gather documentation on SQL dialects and external functions, as shown in Tab. <a href="#A2.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ B.7 SQL Dialect Documents Collection ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>.
Additionally, for Spider 2.0, we preserve the original codebase of the SQL-related project.
For Spider 2.0, besides collecting reference documents, annotators also gather resources such as codebases, database interfaces to establish the context for each task (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
Since some complex data transformation intentions may not be fully captured by a natural language question, annotators provide additional context, including data model descriptions (App.<a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>) or predefined answer files (App.<a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Examples of Context Setup ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>), to maintain clarity while addressing potential ambiguities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4) Natural language task instructions annotation.</span>
Annotators are required to write questions based on the SQLs and context gathered in Step 3, crafting two versions for different settings.
The instructions are designed to balance both <span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">naturalness</span> and <span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unambiguity</span>.
Due to the differences between Spider 2.0 and Spider 2.0-lite/snow, code agent tasks demonstrate greater naturalness in its questions because it provides contexts and predefined files to guide the answers, while text-to-SQL tasks prioritize unambiguity, ensuring clearer and more straightforward specifications (see App.<a href="#A2.SS6" title="B.6 The difference in task instructions between Spider 2.0 and Spider 2.0-lite. ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.6</span></a> for differences).
Annotators manually write the instructions, making them natural by <span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">avoiding blunt descriptions</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">removing ambiguity</span> in the expected results, and ensuring that all SQL <span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">conditions are clearly mentioned</span>.
Also, the DBT-project tasks (see Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and App.<a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>), which are realistic data transformation coding scenarios, are exclusively used in Spider 2.0. Annotators craft task instructions based on the provided context. After the initial annotation, they verify the semantic equivalence between the SQL queries and instructions, paraphrasing for clarity with the help of LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5) Execution-based focused evaluation.</span>
In this step, annotators are required to obtain results from the databases programmatically and write evaluation scripts (details in App.<a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Spider 2.0 Evaluation Scripts ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>).
The evaluation scripts can process the results in the form of strings, tables, and database files. It is important to note that in table-based evaluations, predicted results may include numerous columns, which might not exactly match the gold standard answers. This discrepancy often arises because some questions do not specify the columns that should be returned.
To mitigate this, the evaluation scripts are specifically focused on the essential components of the answers, ignoring non-essential columns and emphasizing the core elements outlined in the instructions.
This method facilitates targeted assessments of key columns for each task, thus significantly reducing the occurrence of false negatives.
For Spider 2.0-lite and Spider 2.0-snow, these settings require that the output must be SQL, so the evaluation will compare the execution results of the SQLs using the table-based assessment method.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6) Quality control.</span>
To ensure the quality of our benchmark, each instruction, the gold SQL query, and evaluation script are reviewed by at least three annotators. We require the annotators to repeatedly review steps 3), 4), and 5) to ensure the correctness, naturalness, and unambiguity of the annotations.
Consequently, 45% of the examples have errors identified by the first validators. After discussions and corrections, following the second round of iteration with the second validators, only 5% of the examples contain errors.
Then we correct all errors and refine all annotations, and ultimately, all examples are deemed fully annotated.
Additionally, we perform a “red team” assessment of our automatic evaluation by providing a set of false results to determine if they would be correctly classified as false, along with various correctly formatted results to verify their classification as true.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Dataset Statistics</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present a detailed statistical analysis of the features of Spider 2.0, Spider 2.0-snow and Spider 2.0-lite,
comparing them with multiple previous datasets in Tab. <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>,
our datasets demonstrate strong complexity and realism in aspects such as databases, SQLs, and task scenarios.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Statistical comparison among Spider 2.0, Spider 2.0-snow and Spider 2.0-lite, and other text-to-SQL benchmarks. Tok. and Func. refer to tokens and functions, respectively. * denotes the statistics from dev set due to the inaccessibility of test set. For more statistics, refer to App.<a href="#A2.SS8" title="B.8 Extend Dataset Statistic ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.8</span></a>.

<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diverse database systems and SQL dialects.</span>
As shown in Fig. <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and Tab. <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, our benchmarks feature a diverse array of database systems, including cloud data warehouses like <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">BigQuery</span> and <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Snowflake</span>, locally hosted databases such as <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Postgres</span> and <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ClickHouse</span>, and lightweight systems like <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">SQLite</span> and <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">DuckDB</span>. This diversity distinguishes our benchmarks from previous work by encompassing various SQL dialects. Notably, 85.98% of the examples require the use of specialized functions from these dialects, with an average of 7.1 special functions utilized in each ground-truth SQL.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Real and complex database schema.</span>
As shown in Tab. <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the databases in Spider 2.0 are equipped with large-scale schemas comprising extensive tables and columns, effectively mirroring real-world enterprise environments.
As shown in Tab. <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, these databases are characterized by complex schema structures (e.g., multiple and nested schemas, partitioned tables; see Fig. <a href="#A2.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ B.3 Spider 2.0 Database Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> and Fig. <a href="#A2.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ B.3 Spider 2.0 Database Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>), and dynamic tables that are updated daily.
Additionally, the data encompasses a broad spectrum of complex types (Fig. <a href="#A2.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ B.8 Extend Dataset Statistic ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>), extensive volumes, and diverse scopes (Fig. <a href="#A2.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ B.8 Extend Dataset Statistic ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>), rendering it more diverse than previous datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Challenging tasks across the data engineering pipeline.</span>
The examples in our benchmarks are collected from real tutorials and forums, covering a wide range of issues encountered in data pipelines, including data wrangling, data transformation, and data analysis (see App.<a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 SQL Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a> for examples).
The difficulty of these questions significantly exceeds that of previous SQL-related benchmarks,
as the SQL queries in Spider 2.0 contain significantly more columns, tokens, and functions per query than those in prior work (see Tab. <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and Fig. <a href="#A2.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ B.8 Extend Dataset Statistic ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> for examples).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Real projects scenarios with codebases and documents.</span>
As demonstrated in Tab. <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and  <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ 2 Benchmark Construction ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, tasks in both datasets require access to documentation, like external knowledge (App.<a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Examples of External Documents ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>) and SQL dialect (App.<a href="#A2.SS7" title="B.7 SQL Dialect Documents Collection ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.7</span></a>), necessitating a deep understanding of these resources.
Compared to other prior works, for each task in Spider 2.0, we provide a codebase context to simulate a real workflow (App.<a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Examples of Context Setup ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>).
More notably, some tasks introduce innovations such as project-level data transformation workflows built on DBT (App.<a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>), a widely used tool for managing data transformations and analytics engineering.
Successfully addressing these tasks requires navigating complex project codebases and databases, comprehending documentation, processing intricate contexts, and generating diverse queries through multi-step execution and reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation metrics.</span>
For Spider 2.0, we use the <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Success Rate (SR)</span> metric, which measures the proportion of task instances successfully completed.
For Spider 2.0-lite and Spider 2.0-snow, the output for each task must be an SQL, we use the widely used metric <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Execution Accuracy (EX)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">(</span><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">)</span></cite></span>.
We employ the execution-based <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">focused</span> evaluation (App.<a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Spider 2.0 Evaluation Scripts ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>) to determine the success of each result for Spider 2.0 and assess the accuracy of SQL execution results for Spider 2.0-lite.
The evaluation scripts are designed to accept output in the form of strings, tables, or database.
For each example, an evaluation script is run for each example, producing a score of either 0 or 1.
It is worth noting that in table-based evaluations, predicted results may contain numerous columns, leading to results that are not exactly the same as the gold answer. This occurs because, for some examples, questions do not explicitly specify which columns to return.
The evaluation scripts are specifically focused on the essential components of the answers, disregarding irrelevant columns and concentrating on the core elements specified in the instructions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Difficulty level.</span>
We tokenize the gold SQL queries based on whitespace and classify their difficulty according to the number of tokens:
<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;80</annotation></semantics></math> tokens as Easy, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80-159" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>159</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80-159</annotation></semantics></math> as Medium, and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 160" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>160</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 160</annotation></semantics></math> as Hard<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            While there are various ways to measure difficulty, we use SQL length here as the most common and significant metric for experimental reference.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLMs.</span>
We experiment with state-of-the-art LLMs, including open-source representatives such as DeepseekCoder-V2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2024</a>)</cite> and Llama-3.1-405B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meta AI, 2024</a>)</cite>, and closed-source ones including Gemini-Pro-1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reid et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Claude-3.5-Sonnet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024</a>)</cite> and GPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2023</a>)</cite> families (GPT-4o, GPT-4, o1-preview and o3-mini).
Follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we use a temperature of 0.0
and truncate from the beginning of the input if still exceeding the max tokens limit required by the models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Code agent frameworks.</span>
We utilize several state-of-the-art frameworks, which have demonstrated excellent performance on other benchmarks. These include Reflexion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, CodeR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, AutoEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Inspired by React <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and Intercode <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, we develop an agent framework called Spider-Agent, which is primarily focused on database-related coding tasks and projects.
The framework allows for multi-turn interactions with the database via command-line interfaces until the final answer is obtained.
The implementation details of Spider-Agent are shown in App.<a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Spider-Agent framework ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text-to-SQL methods.</span>
We also evaluate several state-of-the-art and widely recognized text-to-SQL methods, including approaches based on prompting LLMs such as DIN-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pourreza &amp; Rafiei, 2024</a>)</cite>, DAIL-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and CHESS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Talaei et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, alongside SFT CodeS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, which fine-tuned open-source models on extensive text-to-SQL corpora.
DAIL-SQL and CHESS achieve the best performance among all accessible methods on the Spider 1.0 and <span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Bird</span> benchmark, respectively.
During implementation, we optimize the prompt organizations across all methods to better align with tasks, incorporating sampled cell values, external knowledge, and SQL dialect specifications (see Fig. <a href="#A3.F22" title="Figure 22 ‣ C.2 Details of Spider 2.0-lite Experiments ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Existing LLMs are still far from being expert on real-world text-to-SQL workflow tasks.</span>
As shown in Tab.<a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and Tab.<a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we used Spider-Agent and its variants to conduct tests on Spider 2.0, Spider 2.0-Lite, and Spider 2.0-Snow.
The o1-preview and o3-mini achieve the highest performance, with a peak success rate of 23.77% on Spider 2.0-snow and 23.40% on Spider 2.0-lite, indicating significant potential for further improvement. It surpasses both GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet across the <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Easy</span>, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Medium</span>, and <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hard</span> cases, highlighting its superior reasoning capabilities.
The open-source LLM DeepSeek-V3 showed a performance of 8.78%, still has significant room for improvement. The results shown in Tab.<a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, combined with the DBT project examples, also exhibit a similar trend.
Tab. <a href="#S3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> illustrates that Spider 2.0-lite and Spider 2.0-snow present significant challenges for traditional text-to-SQL methods. The highest performing method, DAIL-SQL + GPT-4o, achieves an EX of only 5.68%, which is markedly lower compared to its score of 86.6% on Spider 1.0 and 57.4% on <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Bird</span> datasets.
With efficiently filtering the minimal sufficient schema, CHESS + GPT-4o is able to tackle more instances than DIN-SQL.
Despite being extensively fine-tuned, SFT CodeS-15B is far from solving Spider 2.0-lite, with an EX score of only 0.73%, which further reveals the significant complexity gap between Spider 2.0-lite and the current text-to-SQL corpus.
For Spider 2.0-snow, even the best method achieves only 2.20% EX, highlighting the increased challenge due to SQL dialect differences.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T5" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>

<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Existing code agent frameworks struggle with solving database-related coding tasks.</span>
Tab.<a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and Tab. <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> show that the current agent frameworks are still unable to effectively address the tasks.
The challenge is that they must not only explore the codebase and documentation, but also navigate complex databases and generate SQL queries that are far more intricate than typical code. This demands a high level of code grounding capability.
Spider-Agent provides a crucial baseline for Spider 2.0, facilitating the evaluation of various LLMs, underscoring the potential for significant advancements and inspiring methodology enhancements for future research.
We also observe that the model must be proficient in debugging from SQL execution feedback and exploring the schemas of different types of databases (e.g., Snowflake), which poses a significant challenge to the code agent’s capabilities.
There is still significant room for improvement in Spider-Agent when it comes to enterprise-level SQL tasks, in order to fully unleash LLMs’ text-to-SQL capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Analysis</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Analysis of Different Task Types</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM-agent frameworks struggle interpreting databases with nested schema.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:30%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Model performance on databases with nested columns in non-dbt projects.</figcaption>
<div id="S4.T6.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:119.2pt;height:21.9pt;vertical-align:-9.5pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-41.7pt,7.7pt) scale(0.588548692517681,0.588548692517681) ;">
<table id="S4.T6.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T6.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">Task Subset</td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">% of Total</td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">SR (↑)</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T6.2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">w/ Nested Column</td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">18.51%</td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">10.34%</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T6.2.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">w/o Nested Columns</td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">68.04%</td>
<td id="S4.T6.2.1.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">27.38%</td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Tab. <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.1 Analysis of Different Task Types ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, the model often performs poorly when handling columns with nested types.
Nested columns are a common scenario in industrial-grade databases (see Fig. <a href="#A2.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ B.3 Spider 2.0 Database Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>), where data is stored in array, dict formats within a single column. This poses significant challenges for LLMs in understanding the schema. As shown in Fig. <a href="#A3.F30" title="Figure 30 ‣ C.6 Case Study of Spider-Agent ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">30</span></a>, LLMs encounter schema linking errors due to an incomplete understanding of the information contained within nested fields.
Most databases with nested types face the issue that models find it difficult to fully grasp the function of each nested column’s internal information, while humans can comprehend the schema through multi-step reasoning and iterative understanding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The performance drops when external documents are required.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T7" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:30%;">

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">From Tab. <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.1 Analysis of Different Task Types ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, we observe that when tasks involve external documents, the model performs poorly, correctly answering only 11 examples out of full dataset that accounts for just 11.54%.
Through error analysis, we find that the model is not incapable of grounding complex documents information. These models typically have the correct problem-solving strategies and effectively explore the database, but fails at the most crucial step: grounding the complex requirements from the documents into SQLs. As the document shown in Fig. <a href="#A2.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ B.4 Examples of External Documents ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, the gold SQL is shown in Tab. <a href="#A2.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>. The failure case shows that the model cannot combine complex document with schema information and convert it into SQL query (Fig. <a href="#A3.F29" title="Figure 29 ‣ C.6 Case Study of Spider-Agent ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">29</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T8" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:30%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Performance on DBT Project.</figcaption>

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM-agent frameworks struggle to address project-level tasks.</span>
As shown in Tab. <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.1 Analysis of Different Task Types ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, the LM agent’s performance on DBT-based project tasks is poor, solving only 12.82% of tasks with just 10 examples correct. This underscores the challenges in there tasks, which can be attributed to: (1) Data transformation projects often require <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">multiple SQL queries</span> to complete various models, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of the project. (2) These tasks involve <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">complex context usage</span>, demanding strong repository exploratory capabilities. (3) Data is stored in databases, requiring the agent to transform data while exploring existing data, alongside SQL coding.
Fig. <a href="#A3.F27" title="Figure 27 ‣ C.6 Case Study of Spider-Agent ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">27</span></a> illustrates the action process of o1-preview successfully solving a task defined in App.<a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>, while Fig. <a href="#A3.F28" title="Figure 28 ‣ C.6 Case Study of Spider-Agent ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">28</span></a> is a failure case due to the failure to explore the information in the “mrr.md” file to solve a monthly recurring revenue classification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Error Analysis of SQL Generation</h3>

<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:30%;">
<div id="S4.F5.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:119.2pt;height:118.9pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-327.5pt,326.5pt) scale(0.154036636148763,0.154036636148763) ;"><img src="2411.07763v2/lite-error-pie.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="width:77.081em; height:77.183em;aspect-ratio:1280/1282;" width="1280" height="1282" alt="Refer to caption">
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Statistics of errors. For detailed descriptions and examples of each error category, see App.<a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Details of Error Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct a detailed analysis of the errors encountered by both code agent frameworks on randomly sampled 300 examples, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Error Analysis of SQL Generation ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
Representative errors along with their statistics and causal analysis are as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Erroneous data analysis (35.5%).</span>
Compare to the previous benchmarks, Spider 2.0 and Spider 2.0-lite exhibit significantly complex data analysis demands that challenge the models’ capabilities:
1) Dialect function usage (10.3%). This includes processing temporal (e.g., <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">DATE_TRUNC</span>) or geographic data (e.g., <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ST_DISTANCE</span>). These functions require a nuanced understanding, which the models often fail to exhibit.
2) Advanced data calculation (7.5%). Model struggle with tasks like grouping samples to analyze trends within groups (using <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">NTILE</span>), or applying formulas for statistical values (e.g., <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CORR</span> for Pearson correlation coefficients; <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">STDDEV</span> for standard deviation).
3) Intricate query planning (17.7%). Gold SQLs typically involve multiple nested queries, intermediate result processing through common table expressions (CTEs), or merging results from various sub-queries via set operations. However, models often inadequately handle these complexities.
Refer to Fig. <a href="#S4.F6.fig1" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Error Analysis of SQL Generation ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> for case studies on erroneous data processing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Wrong schema linking (27.6%).</span>
This category includes errors with wrong tables and columns.
For column linking errors (16.6%), the average number of columns per database in Spider 2.0-lite far exceeds those in other benchmarks (over <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="755" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>755</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">755</annotation></semantics></math> compared to approximately <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="54" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>54</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">54</annotation></semantics></math> in <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Bird</span>), making accurate column linking extremely challenging. Regarding table linking (10.1%), although examples from BigQuery support advanced syntax features like (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TABLE_SUFFIX</span>) and wildcard expressions, the models show limited flexibility in leveraging these features, even in few-shot setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JOIN errors (8.3%).</span> While foreign keys represent known schema relationships essential for valid SQL JOIN operations, databases in BigQuery often lack explicit foreign key. This omission forces models to infer potential keys based on column names and descriptions, leading to errors.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T10" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.T10.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:190.8pt;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Table 9: </span>EX for baseline methods on Spider 2.0-lite under oracle setting. To seek the highest possible performance, we also employ the latest o1-preview as the base LLM.</figcaption>

</span></div>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<figure id="S4.F6.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:397.5pt;"><img src="2411.07763v2/lite-case-study.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/347;" width="548" height="347" alt="Refer to caption">

(a): An example of <span id="S4.F6.fig1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">incorrect data calculation</span>, where quantiles were incorrectly divided based on the number of trips, rather than on the <span id="S4.F6.fig1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trip duration</span> as required.
(b): An example of <span id="S4.F6.fig1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">incorrect planning</span>, where the predicted SQL incorrectly sorted data by the number of users, rather than by the required <span id="S4.F6.fig1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">retention ratio</span>. The prerequisite for achieving this is to properly plan a sequence of CTEs.
Additional examples of error cases across all categories are available in Fig. <a href="#A3.F23" title="Figure 23 ‣ C.3 Details of Error Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a> and Fig. <a href="#A3.F24" title="Figure 24 ‣ C.3 Details of Error Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">24</span></a>.
</figcaption>
