</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Analysis of Different Experimental Settings</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Providing oracle functions leads to a slight performance improvement.</span>
Considering that Spider 2.0 and Spider 2.0-lite involve SQL dialects from various database systems, we provide syntax and function documentation for each system to prevent the methods from suffering due to lack of syntax knowledge. For each example, we manually include the relevant function documentation that may be required, eliminating the need for a retrieval method and ensuring that the necessary syntax knowledge is readily accessible.
As shown in Tab. <a href="#S4.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 4.2 Error Analysis of SQL Generation ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, providing oracle SQL function documentation results in only a slight improvement in model performance. This suggests that, to a certain extent, models are capable of selecting appropriate functions and understanding their basic usage and syntax. However, the critical challenge lies in accurately utilizing these functions to reflect user intentions, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S4.F6.fig1" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Error Analysis of SQL Generation ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(a).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Few-shot prompting has little impact on performance.</span>
Spider 2.0-lite is not divided into train and dev sets, we manually select representative examples from the same SQL dialect as the SQL to be predicted, with distinct characteristics (encompassing multiple CTE or nested queries, or requiring intricate data processing) to serve as few-shot examples.
Unexpectedly, few-shot in-context learning shows only marginal improvements in performance (see Tab. <a href="#S4.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 4.2 Error Analysis of SQL Generation ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>).
This may be due to the gap between the simplistic text-to-SQL pre-training data used with LLMs and the complexity of the few-shot examples. Additionally, extensive schema prompts may hinder the model’s ability to effectively assimilate information in the few-shot examples.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Code generation and text-to-SQL benchmark.</span>
As model capabilities advance, code generation benchmarks have become more complex and generalized. Many benchmarks (e.g., SQL-Spider <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, Bash-NL2Bash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, Python-HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>) treat code generation as seq2seq tasks.
Many previous works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jing et al., 2024</a>)</cite> define code generation tasks for data science.
MLAgentBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and Intercode <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> focus on interactive environments, while SWE-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2023</a>)</cite> emphasizes repository-level coding tasks.
Spider2-V <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> proposes data science and engineering benchmark in a multimodal setting.
Many previous datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hazoom et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> have made significant contributions to the advancement of text-to-SQL tasks.
However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks primarily target lightweight local databases, much smaller in schema scale and data volume than cluster-hosted industrial databases, and fail to capture the <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">agentic</span> nature of SQL programming using various dialects in real scenarios.
Spider 2.0 bridges the gap between research and enterprise-level industrial text-to-SQL workflows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Code agent framework and text-to-SQL methods.</span>
The intersection of generative code models and interactive problem-solving has spurred significant advancements in both agent-based frameworks and text-to-SQL methodologies. Recent efforts aim to enhance the reasoning capabilities of language models, as evidenced by a surge in agent methods designed for code generation tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Several works have designed special actions to standardize agent operations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
For methods specifically designed for text-to-SQL, several fine-tuning methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>
and LLM-prompting methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Talaei et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pourreza &amp; Rafiei, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> have achieved strong performance on previous benchmarks.
We propose Spider-Agent, a code agent framework specifically designed for database-related tasks, showcasing strong performance in this domain. For Spider 2.0-lite, we also adapt several text-to-SQL methods to suit our benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose Spider 2.0, a benchmark for real-world enterprise-level text-to-SQL workflow tasks. It encompasses diverse database systems with various SQL dialects, large and complex database schemas, and challenging tasks across the data engineering pipeline, all set within real project scenarios including codebases and documentation. Despite being the most advanced LLMs (o1-preview), they still perform poorly on Spider 2.0, achieving a success rate of only 21.3%, which underscores its status as a highly challenging benchmark. Spider 2.0 presents a novel challenge for text-to-SQL research, providing a direction towards more realistic and intelligent solutions.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Spider 2.0 Evaluation Scripts</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the detailed definition and discussion of evaluation metrics
for Spider 2.0-lite and Spider 2.0.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spider 2.0-lite.</span> The setting of Spider 2.0-lite resembles that of a traditional text-to-SQL task in which text-to-SQL parsers are required to generate SQL queries. Therefore, <span id="A1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Execution Accuracy(EX)</span> is used as the primary evaluation metric. Slightly different from existing works, we employ an <span id="A1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">execution-based focused evaluation</span>, which measures whether all columns in the gold value are present in the output of the predicted SQL query. This is defined as follows:</p>
<table id="A1.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_gather ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle{\rm EX}=\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbbm{1}(v^{n},\hat{v}^{n})}{N}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>EX</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mn>𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle{\rm EX}=\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbbm{1}(v^{n},\hat{v}^{n})}{N},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A1.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{where}\quad\mathbbm{1}(v,\hat{v})=\begin{cases}1,\ \mathrm{if}\;v_{i}\in\hat{v},\forall v_{i}\in v\\
0,\ \mathrm{if}\;v_{i}\notin\hat{v},\exists v_{i}\in v\end{cases}\!\!\!\!\!\!," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>where</mi><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mn>𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mrow><mi>if</mi><mo lspace="0.280em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mrow><mi>if</mi><mo lspace="0.280em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>∉</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∃</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{where}\quad\mathbbm{1}(v,\hat{v})=\begin{cases}1,\ \mathrm{if}\;v_{i}\in\hat{v},\forall v_{i}\in v\\
0,\ \mathrm{if}\;v_{i}\notin\hat{v},\exists v_{i}\in v\end{cases}\!\!\!\!\!\!,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the <math id="A1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th column of data frame <math id="A1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> denote execution results of the gold SQL and predicted SQL for the <math id="A1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-th instance in the evaluation set, respectively.
Empirically, this evaluation method significantly reduces the false negative rate without increasing the number of false positives. Given that the ground-truth values result from extensive data wrangling, transformation, and analysis, it is difficult for models to manipulate or exploit the system.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spider 2.0.</span> We use the <span id="A1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Success rate (SR)</span>, which measures the proportion of task instances successfully resolved. Human-written evaluation scripts are used to determine whether an example is resolved. For each example, we provide string-based, table-based, and database-based evaluation functions, depending on the type of answer output, as shown in Tab. <a href="#A1.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix A Spider 2.0 Evaluation Scripts ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Examples.</span> Maintaining naturalness and unambiguity is often a conflicting challenge. To address this, we provide an example to illustrate the important parameters “condition_cols” and “ignore_order”. Achieving a balance between these two aspects is quite challenging, which is why we incorporate this mechanism into our evaluation scripts.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Given a data frame <math id="A1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> with a set of column vectors <math id="A1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{v_{i}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{v_{i}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, each representing the cell values for the <math id="A1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th column, a prediction <math id="A1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}</annotation></semantics></math> is considered equivalent with <math id="A1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> if and only if for any <math id="A1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}\in v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}\in v</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}\in\hat{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}\in\hat{v}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Therefore, at such times, we only check whether a specific column appears in it.
Intuitively, if all columns in the reference table appear in the result table, the result is considered correct.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">For example, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix A Spider 2.0 Evaluation Scripts ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, the question does not explicitly specify which columns are required in our response. Consider the following question: <span id="A1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“The company management has requested a detailed report on the year-to-date performance of the Magnificent 7 stocks.”</span>.
We need to carefully analyze the task requirements and only check if the following columns in the reference answer—<span id="A1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“Ticker”</span>, <span id="A1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“Change<math id="A1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\_" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\_</annotation></semantics></math>YTD”</span>—appear in the predicted answer. This meets the semantic requirements of the abstract instruction.
Empirically, we find our evaluation metric is reliable in identifying solutions with alternative output, with a relatively low false-negative rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/evaluation_examples.png" id="A1.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:384/182;" width="384" height="182" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>An example of evaluation scripts for table-based evaluation: in this example, the <span id="A1.F7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">condition_cols</span> is <math id="A1.F7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,5\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,5\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the <span id="A1.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ignore_order</span> is <math id="A1.F7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="true" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">true</annotation></semantics></math>. As long as these two columns are predicted correctly, the example can be considered solved.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.T11" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 11: </span>The evaluation scripts for Spider 2.0 are tailored to the specific format of the model’s output. Each script is optimized to handle various output types, ensuring precise and contextually appropriate evaluation.</figcaption>
<div id="A1.T11.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:397.5pt;height:853.8pt;vertical-align:-424.4pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-2.9pt,6.2pt) scale(0.985779082214519,0.985779082214519) ;">

<span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:56.9pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output Type</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Description</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:227.6pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parameters</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T11.2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:56.9pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">String</span> 
<br class="ltx_break">w/o number</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If the answer is found in the string, it is given a score of 1; otherwise, it receives a score of 0.</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:227.6pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">pred</span> (str): The string in which to search for substrings.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">gold</span> (List of str): A list of strings to check within the predicted string.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">conj</span> (str): The conjunction used for matching (‘and’ or ‘or’). Default is ‘or’.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.2.3.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">exclude</span> (List of Str): Strings that must not be present in the answer.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T11.2.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:56.9pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">String</span> 
<br class="ltx_break">w. number</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For output strings containing numbers, the script captures these numbers and performs number matching for scoring using the <span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">number_match</span> function.</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:227.6pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">pred</span> (str): The string in which to search for substrings.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">gold</span> (List[str<span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">|</span>float]): A list of strings or numbers to check within the predicted string.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">percentage</span> (bool): Default is false. If the gold answer is related to percentages, set this to true for more robust evaluation.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">precision</span> (int): The number of decimal places to consider. Defaults to 4.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.3.3.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">conj</span> (str): The conjunction used for matching (‘and’ or ‘or’). Default is ‘or’, and it’s typically ‘or’.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T11.2.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:56.9pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Table</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If the answer is a CSV file or a table in string format, table-level evaluation is performed.</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:227.6pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">result</span> (str): Path to the CSV file or result string.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">gold</span> (str <span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">|</span> List[str]): Path(s) to the gold file(s), excluding the root directory. Multiple potential gold answers are supported.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">condition_cols</span> (List[int] <span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">|</span> List[List[int]]): List of column indices to match conditions. For example, [0, 1] uses the 0th and 1st columns in the gold table for matching, while ignoring the others.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.4.3.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ignore_order</span> (bool): Whether to ignore the order of rows when matching elements.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T11.2.1.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:56.9pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Database</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If the answer is stored in a DB file, database-level evaluation is applied using the <span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">db_match</span> function.</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:227.6pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">result</span> (str): Path to the DuckDB file containing the result tables.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">gold</span> (str): Path to the DuckDB file containing the gold standard tables.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">condition_tabs</span> (List[str], optional): List of table names to be checked. If not provided, all tables in the gold DuckDB file will be considered.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">condition_cols</span> (List[List[int]], optional): A list of lists, where each inner list contains column indices used for matching conditions for the corresponding table. Defaults to considering all columns.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.5.3.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ignore_orders</span> (List[bool], optional): A list of boolean values indicating whether to ignore the row order for each table comparison. Defaults to [False] for each table.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T11.2.1.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:56.9pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SQL</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If the output is an SQL, execution-based evaluation is used. This is primarily designed for Spider 2.0-lite.</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A1.T11.2.1.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:227.6pt;">
<span id="A1.T11.2.1.6.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">To compare the execution results of the predicted SQL and the gold SQL, table matching is used.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>

</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Annotation Details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>SQL Annotation Examples</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present several representative examples of the SQL annotation process, including the original SQL, how the SQL was rewritten to obtain the gold SQL, and the use of external knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tab. <a href="#A2.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> presents an example based on the Google Analytics database. The task is to calculate the source of web traffic and count the number of sessions for each traffic channel within a given time period.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Tab. <a href="#A2.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> presents an example based on New York City public data, where the task is to find Citibike and taxi trips between specified locations and analyze whether Citibike or taxi is more suitable for travel between the two locations. In this case, the condition in the original SQL is to calculate trips between the two locations by Citibike and car. We extend this condition by introducing a real-life problem: identifying which routes are faster by Citibike compared to taxi.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Tab. <a href="#A2.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> is based on the Google Patents database, which contains a large amount of patent information. The original SQL applied several filtering conditions to retrieve a set of patents. We find a document explaining how to calculate a patent’s originality score, which led to an advanced calculation method. As a result, the final task include additional complex calculation steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Tab. <a href="#A2.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> is also based on the Google Analytics database. The original SQL calculates the Product List Page (PLP) and Product Details Page (PDP). Based on the description in the blog, we define a new task to calculate the conversion rate by determining the probability of users clicking from PLP to PDP.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Tab. <a href="#A2.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> presents an example where we merge and rewrite two related SQL queries. The first SQL calculates the 50 weather stations closest to downtown Chicago, while the second SQL calculates the number of bike trips on rainy and non-rainy days in New York City. We combine these two tasks, meaning that to determine whether it is a rainy day, we first need to find data from the weather station closest to downtown New York City.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>DBT Project Annotation Examples</h3>

<figure id="A2.F8" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:47%;"><img src="2411.07763v2/figures/dbt_codebase.jpg" id="A2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:250/273;" width="250" height="273" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Codebase for a DBT project, showing models, macros, and configuration files.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Annotation Pipeline of DBT Project.</span>
The DBT project can be found on online resources and is one of the projects with the most SQL scripts. Similar data transformation tools are widely used in industrial production. Completing a DBT project requires a comprehensive understanding of both the code and documentation within the project to accomplish the entire task.
Fig. <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows a Salesforce-based project in Spider 2.0.
This represents a natural and realistic SQL generation scenario. Using a Fivetran Salesforce transformation package <span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/fivetran/dbt_salesforce/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/fivetran/dbt_salesforce/</a></span></span></span> as an example, we transform a complex DBT project into a Spider 2.0 example through the following steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">(1) Run a DBT project from start to finish, ensuring it is bug-free and generates a dbt DAG (Fig. <a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>). This allows for a comprehensive understanding of the data flow.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">(2) The DBT project includes yml files and markdown documents, where the project developers have already planned out the data models and data flow. We will use these as the basis for task instructions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">(3) We remove the .sql files corresponding to a specific data flow within the complete DBT project. For example, in Fig. <a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we may delete one to three data flows, as shown in Fig. <a href="#A2.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, removing “sales_daily_activity” and “salesforce_contact_enhanced” along with their upstream nodes. This turns it into an incomplete transformation project. Note that the DAG figure is only used as an aid for data annotation, and the task does not include any images.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">(4) Write the task instructions. For instance, we can draft a prompt like, “I need a daily report on key sales activities—covering tasks completed, events held, leads generated, and the status of opportunities.” Although the data model contains many columns, thanks to the presence of yml files (see Fig. <a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>), there is no need to describe the output columns in detail in the instructions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/figures/dbt_yml.jpg" id="A2.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/535;" width="548" height="535" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>This is a common configuration file in DBT projects used to define the schema of a data model. It represents a natural SQL generation scenario, specifying details such as field names, data types, and references for the “salesforce_opportunity_enhanced” data model.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/figures/dbt-dag.png" id="A2.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/206;" width="548" height="206" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) illustrating the data flow and dependencies between various Salesforce tables and models in a dbt (data build tool) project. The graph shows stages of transformation, from raw Salesforce data (green nodes) to enhanced and aggregated models (blue nodes), representing different entities such as opportunities, contacts, accounts, and events.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/figures/dbt-dag_new.png" id="A2.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/233;" width="548" height="233" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>In this version of the DAG, several data models are missing, including “salesforce_daily_activity” and “salesforce_contact_enhanced” along with their upstream nodes. This creates an incomplete data flow compared to the original.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Approach to Solving DBT Project Examples.</span>
As shown in Fig. <a href="#A3.F27" title="Figure 27 ‣ C.6 Case Study of Spider-Agent ‣ Appendix C Details of Experiments ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">27</span></a>, completing a DBT project example typically requires the following abilities:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">1) Problem comprehension. First, it is necessary to fully understand a natural language task.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">2) Project reading ability. A real-world data transformation project consists of multiple files, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. The method needs to explore the codebase and review relevant project files, including <span id="A2.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.yml</span>, <span id="A2.SS2.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.md</span>, and <span id="A2.SS2.p8.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.sql</span> files. YML files (Fig. <a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>) generally define the data models for the data transformation, <span id="A2.SS2.p8.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.md</span> files contain textual descriptions of the data models, and SQL files are the data transformation models themselves.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">3) Database exploration ability. The codebase only contains the data transformation code, while the data to be transformed is stored in a database. The method must explore the database to understand the available source data and identify any missing data models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">4) Problem localization ability. By combining the natural language problem and the YML files, the method should locate where to add or modify the code in the project.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p11.1" class="ltx_p">5) Coding ability. The method needs to complete complex data transformation code based on the data models defined in the YML files and add the .sql files in the appropriate locations. Visually, it requires completing the data models defined in the yml file, transitioning from Fig. <a href="#A2.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> to Fig. <a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p12" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p12.1" class="ltx_p">6) Data transformation execution. Once the SQL is written, it is necessary to run <span id="A2.SS2.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dbt run</span> to execute the data transformation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p13" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p13.1" class="ltx_p">7) Debugging. After running the DBT project, if the data transformation is successful, the data models (the tables) in the database will change, with tables being added or removed. The method needs to examine the database to determine if the transformation was fully successful. If not, the above steps must be repeated until the method meets the problem’s requirements.</p>
</div>

<figure id="A2.T14" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 14: </span>Google patent example, <span id="A2.T14.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">advanced calculation</span> surface rewrite.</figcaption>
<table id="A2.T14.4" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A2.T14.4.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T14.4.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="A2.T14.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T14.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.T14.4.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Question</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T14.4.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T14.4.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T14.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T14.4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">What is the publication number of US patent granted at January 2018, with the highest originality score based on the diversity of 4-digits IPC codes from its backward citations?</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T14.4.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T14.4.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T14.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T14.4.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.T14.4.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Reference Plan</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T14.4.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T14.4.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T14.4.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T14.4.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">1. Filter US Patents: Select publication numbers and application numbers from the dataset, including only records where the country code is ’US’, the grant date is within January 2018, and excluding records with a grant date of 0. Additionally, only consider patents with a specific kind code pattern (e.g., %B2%).
2. Extract IPC Codes: Select the publication number and count the unique 4-digit IPC codes associated with each selected patent.
3. Identify Maximum IPC Code Count: Create a subset of records that have the maximum count of a specific 4-digit IPC code for each patent.
4. Calculate IPC Occurrences in Backward Citations: Join the filtered patents with their backward citations. For each backward citation, join with the subset of records to get the 4-digit IPC codes, counting occurrences of each IPC code in the backward citations for each patent.
5. Compute Originality Score: For each patent, calculate an originality score based on the diversity of the 4-digit IPC codes from the backward citations, using a formula that considers the sum of squared occurrences of each IPC code, normalized by the total number of occurrences.
6. Select Highest Originality Score: From the computed originality scores, select the patent with the highest score.
7. Return Result: Output the publication number of the patent with the highest originality score.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T14.4.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T14.4.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T14.4.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T14.4.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.T14.4.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Gold SQL (After rewriting)</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T14.4.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T14.4.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T14.4.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2411.07763v2/example4_2.svg" id="A2.T14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:491/294;" width="491" height="294"></object>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T14.4.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T14.4.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T14.4.7.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T14.4.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.T14.4.7.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Original SQL</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T14.4.8" class="ltx_tr">

</span></td></tr>
</table>

<span id="A2.T15.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T15.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.T15.4.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Question</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T15.4.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T15.4.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T15.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T15.4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Calculate the conversion rate from product list pages to product detail pages for all sessions at January 2nd, 2021.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T15.4.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T15.4.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T15.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T15.4.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.T15.4.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Reference Plan</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T15.4.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T15.4.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A2.T15.4.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A2.T15.4.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">1. query the event data to retrieve all unique event names
2. Selects events data from the Google Analytics 4 (GA4) sample e-commerce dataset for the specific date (20210102)
3. Filter to include only events named page_view, which represent page views.
4. flatten the nested event_params array and extract values for ga_session_id, ga_session_number, page_title, and page_location. This allows the analysis of individual page views within each user’s session.
5. Further processes the unnested event data to classify pages based on URL depth and specific keywords into either Product Detail Pages (PDP) or Product Listing Pages (PLP).
6. Applies window functions to the categorized data to calculate the previous and next pages for each session per user, facilitating analysis of navigation paths between pages.
7. Filters sessions where the current page is a PLP and the next page is a PDP.
8. Counts the number of sessions transitioning from PLP to PDP and divides this by the total views of PLP pages to calculate the conversion rate.</span>
</span></td></tr>

<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Spider 2.0 Database Examples</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Google Analytics 4 serves as a notable example of a Spider 2.0 database (see Fig. <a href="#A2.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ B.3 Spider 2.0 Database Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>). For each Google Analytics 4 property and linked Firebase project enabled for BigQuery export, a dataset named <span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">analytics_{property_id}</span> is created. Within the dataset, daily tables named <span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">events_YYYYMMDD</span> are generated when the Daily export option is enabled.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To accommodate latency, Google Analytics 4 updates these daily tables for up to three days with late-arriving events, ensuring proper timestamping. Each column in these tables represents specific event parameters, some of which are nested within RECORDS and may be repeated. For instance, the <span id="A2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">item_params</span> RECORD stores custom item parameters unique to each implementation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/ga4_schema.png" id="A2.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/186;" width="494" height="186" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>Google analytics 4 database schema with nested record.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#A2.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ B.3 Spider 2.0 Database Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> showcases an example of an enterprise-level real-world database environment from Spider 2.0, with multiple schemas to navigate through, each of them containing a variety of tables. It highlights the complex structure types of Spider 2.0 databses, which exemplifies how our benchmark encompasses a broader and more intricate variety compared to others.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F13" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/nyc_gsod.png" id="A2.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:411/254;" width="411" height="254" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>Bigquery database environment with multiple schema and tables.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Examples of External Documents</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the external documents utilized in Spider 2.0. The first is a table that outlines the categorization method for traffic channels. The original document provided an HTML table, which we present here in Fig. <a href="#A2.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ B.4 Examples of External Documents ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>. The second document is the Google Page Category as shown in Fig. <a href="#A2.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ B.4 Examples of External Documents ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>, which demonstrates how to classify a page into categories such as Product List Page and Product Detail Page.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F14" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2411.07763v2/figures/ga4_category.png" id="A2.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/217;" width="494" height="217" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span>Channel group of Google Analytics, external document for a bigquery example.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F15" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.F15.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="639.06" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 639.06" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,639.06) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.32 L 0 633.74 C 0 636.68 2.38 639.06 5.32 639.06 L 544.68 639.06 C 547.62 639.06 550 636.68 550 633.74 L 550 5.32 C 550 2.38 547.62 0 544.68 0 L 5.32 0 C 2.38 0 0 2.38 0 5.32 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#D3D3D3;" fill="#D3D3D3" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 5.32 L 1.38 616.12 L 548.62 616.12 L 548.62 5.32 C 548.62 3.15 546.85 1.38 544.68 1.38 L 5.32 1.38 C 3.15 1.38 1.38 3.15 1.38 5.32 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.26 624.13)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:38.41em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="531.49"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:38.41em;">
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Product page category</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.26 11.95)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:38.41em;--ltx-fo-height:43.09em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="599" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 596.31)" width="531.49"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:38.41em;">
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">### Refined Page Classification Criteria</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">#### Overview</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">To enhance our understanding of user engagement on our e-commerce platform, we differentiate between two types of pages based on the URL structure: Product Listing Pages (PLPs) and Product Detail Pages (PDPs). These classifications are crucial for analyzing user behavior and improving site navigation efficiency.</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">#### Product Listing Pages (PLPs)</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">PLPs are identified by specific characteristics in the URL:</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- The URL must be divided into at least five segments.</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- Neither the fourth nor the fifth segment contains a ’+’ sign, ensuring these are
not detail views.</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- The fourth or fifth segment must contain one of the following category names, indicating a broader category or collection page rather than a specific product focus:</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- Accessories
- Apparel
- Brands
- Campus Collection
- Drinkware
- Electronics
- Google Redesign
- Lifestyle
- Nest
- New 2015 Logo
- Notebooks &amp; Journals
- Office
- Shop by Brand
- Small Goods
- Stationery
- Wearables</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">#### Product Detail Pages (PDPs)</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.11.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">PDPs, which focus on individual products, are marked by:</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.12.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- A URL split into at least five segments, akin to PLPs.</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- The presence of a ’+’ sign in the last segment, a common marker for detailed product pages.</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.14" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.14.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- The fourth or fifth segment must also include one of the specified category names, ensuring that the detail being viewed pertains to one of the recognized product categories:</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.15" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.15.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">- Accessories
- Apparel
- Brands
- Campus Collection
- Drinkware
- Electronics
- Google Redesign
- Lifestyle
- Nest
- New 2015 Logo
- Notebooks &amp; Journals
- Office
- Shop by Brand
- Small Goods
- Stationery
- Wearables</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.16" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.16.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">### Conclusion</span></span>
<span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.17" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F15.pic1.2.17.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This detailed classification approach enables a more nuanced analysis of user pathways and interactions on our platform. By distinguishing between general browsing (PLPs) and targeted product interest (PDPs), we can tailor our content and design strategies to better meet the needs of our users, ultimately enhancing the shopping experience and improving business outcomes.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15: </span>Page category document of Google analytics 4.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.5 </span>Examples of Context Setup</h3>

<div id="A2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Besides the context setup method for the DBT project mentioned in App.<a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>, we will outline the process for establishing the context in a example about query database.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the task, <span id="A2.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Can you provide the details of the top 5 longest bike share trips that started during the second half of 2017?</span>, ‘query.py’ serves as our predefined interface for interaction between the model and the cloud database. This question is inherently ambiguous; without specifying the answer format constraints, evaluating the responses becomes challenging. Therefore, we provide “result.csv’, which defines the required answer format.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><pre id="A2.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">|--- README.md   # The task description
|--- query.py    # The query interface
|--- bigquery_credential.json   # Bigquery credentials
‘--- result.csv  # Answer format of data in November 2022

-- result.csv
trip_id,duration_sec,star_date,start_station_name,route,bike_number,
subscriber_type,member_birth_year,age,age_class,member_gender,region_name

</pre>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For the examples presented in Tab. <a href="#A2.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ B.2 DBT Project Annotation Examples ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, we outline the setup details for the Spider 2.0 example. Additionally, we provide answer examples for specific cases, which not only constrain the answer format but also enable the agent to perform self-debugging using these examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The task instruction is <span id="A2.SS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Provide the number of sessions and percentage breakdown by channel for December 2020</span>. We supply ‘202011.csv’ and ‘202101.csv’ as demonstration answers. We envision a real SQL writing scenario where the agent can first query November 2020 to check for consistency with ‘202011.csv’.
If discrepancies arise, the agent can identify that their SQL is incorrect and make the necessary corrections.
Note that this is not a task requirement; it is simply our belief that real SQL writing has such a need, and we will not mandate that the model does this.
We believe this approach reflects a natural and realistic setting, although we only provide answer constraints for a limited number of examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><pre id="A2.SS5.p6.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">|--- README.md   # The task description
|--- query.py    # The query interface
|--- BASIC_SQLs  # SQL examples of google analytics
|--- bigquery_credential.json   # Bigquery credentials
|--- 202012.csv  # The predefined answer file,
|--- 202101.csv  # Answer format of data in January 2021
‘--- 202011.csv  # Answer format of data in November 2022

-- 202011.csv

item_name,item_quantity
Google Decal,103
Google Clear Pen 4-Pack,81
Google Mesh Bag Red,79
Google Mini Kick Ball,77
Google Light Pen Red,8
Google Laptop and Cell Phone Stickers,7
Google Pen Neon Coral,7
Google Metallic Notebook Set,7
Google Pen Lilac,5
Google Pen Red,5


</pre>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The query interface of Bigquery “query.py’ is</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><pre id="A2.SS5.p8.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">import os
import pandas as pd
from google.cloud import bigquery

def query_data(sql_query, is_save, save_path="result.csv"):
    """
    Queries data from BigQuery based on the provided SQL query and handles the result.

    Args:
    sql_query (str): SQL query string to be executed.
    is_save (bool): If True, saves the query results to a CSV file at the specified save_path.
                    If False, prints the results to the console.
    save_path (str): The file path where the results will be saved if is_save is True.
    Defaults to ’result.csv’.
    """
    os.environ["GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"] = "bigquery_credential.json"
    client = bigquery.Client()
    query_job = client.query(sql_query)
    try:
      results = query_job.result().to_dataframe()
      if results.empty:
        print("No data found for the specified query.")
      else:
        if is_save:
            results.to_csv(save_path, index=False)
            print(f"Results saved to {save_path}")
        else:
            print(results)
    except Exception as e:
      print("Error occurred while fetching data: ", e)

if __name__ == "__main__":

   # Write your SQL query in the sql_query variable to interact with the database,
   #example SQL query related to this task is provided below
    sql_query = """
    SELECT
      *
    FROM
      ‘bigquery-public-data.ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce.events_*‘
    WHERE
      _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN ’20201201’ AND ’20201231’
    LIMIT 1
    """
    query_data(sql_query, is_save=True, save_path="result.csv")
</pre>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.6 </span>The difference in task instructions between Spider 2.0 and Spider 2.0-lite.</h3>

<div id="A2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During the annotation process, we found that <span id="A2.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unambiguity</span> and <span id="A2.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">naturalness</span> are two mutually exclusive concepts. Therefore, in Spider 2.0-Lite, we emphasize unambiguity, while in Spider 2.0, we emphasize naturalness. The two instructional approaches restore the possible question forms that may arise in real-world text-to-SQL workflows.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example 1:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Spider 2.0: The company management has requested a detailed report on the year-to-date performance of the Magnificent 7 stocks.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Spider 2.0-lite: Please show the price change rate of the Magnificent 7 stocks from the beginning of this year to today.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example 2:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Spider 2.0: Can you provide the details of the top 5 longest bike share trips that started during the second half of 2017?</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Spider 2.0-lite: Can you provide the details of the top 5 longest bike share trips that started during the second half of 2017, including the trip ID, duration in seconds, start date, start station name, route (start station to end station), bike number, subscriber type, member’s birth year, age, age classification, gender, and the region name of the start station?</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS6.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example 3:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Spider 2.0: What’s the no-tip percentage for NYC yellow taxi trips in each borough from January 1-7, 2016, considering valid trips with at least one passenger and non-negative amounts?</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Spider 2.0-lite: For NYC yellow taxi trips between January 1-7, 2016, could you tell me the percentage of no tips in each borough. Ensure trips where the dropoff occurs after the pickup, the passenger count is greater than 0, and trip distance, tip, tolls, MTA tax, fare, and total amount are non-negative.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.7 </span>SQL Dialect Documents Collection</h3>

<div id="A2.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The core of SQL dialects lies in different advanced functions and subtle syntax variations across SQL versions. To support retrieval-augmented agent frameworks, we crawled and pre-processed the function documents for different database systems from their official websites. The detailed statistics of the crawled web pages and parsed categories/functions are presented in Tab. <a href="#A2.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ B.7 SQL Dialect Documents Collection ‣ Appendix B Annotation Details ‣ Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>. Note that, functions belonging to the same category (e.g., <span id="A2.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">aggregate</span> functions like <span id="A2.SS7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">COUNTIF</span> and <span id="A2.SS7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">STRING_AGG</span>) may be introduced in the same paragraph in some web pages. In this case, we re-use the description on this shared function category for different concrete functions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T17" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 17: </span>Statistics of different database systems on Spider 2.0. Notice that, <sup id="A2.T17.3" class="ltx_sup">†</sup> means there is no well-defined function list in the official web pages for Postgres, thus we merely use the summarized document for each function category.</figcaption>

</figure>
<section id="A2.SS7.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.7.1 </span>Processed Functions for Different Database Systems</h4>

<div id="A2.SS7.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS7.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we demonstrate examples of parsed documents for different database systems. These pre-parsed chunks can be retrieved and inserted into the prompt to compensate agents for their deficiencies in SQL dialect knowledge.</p>
</div>
